A.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement, not the instantaneous value at a point, so it is not what is added at every instant.

B.explanation: The resultant displacement at a point is the vector sum of the individual displacements, allowing constructive and destructive superposition.

C.explanation: Intensity is proportional to $(amplitude)^2$ and does not add directly because displacements can cancel while energy transfer does not cancel in the same way.

D.explanation: Wavelength is set by the source frequency and wave speed and is unchanged when waves cross at a point.

hints: Notice the question says when waves meet at a point - think about the instantaneous shift of the medium from equilibrium at that place and time.
Recall that this shift can be positive on one side and negative on the other, so two waves can reinforce or cancel.
Compare this with intensity and amplitude: intensity depends on the square of the oscillation size, and amplitude is only the maximum size, not the moment-by-moment value that cancels.
walkthrough: Identify what the question asks: the quantity that is vector-added at each point when two or more waves overlap.
State the governing rule: the principle of superposition says the resultant oscillation at a point is the vector sum of the individual oscillations at that instant.

Apply the cause-and-effect: if one wave displaces the particles one way and the other displaces them the same way, the total shift is larger, and if they displace opposite ways, the total shift is smaller or zero.

Distinguish the distractors: amplitude describes only the peak size, intensity describes power per unit area proportional to $(amplitude)^2$, and wavelength describes the spatial period - none of these add linearly at a point.
Therefore the added quantity is the instantaneous displacement. This is option B.
